title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Painting
audience: Owners of small Australian painting businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill for painting work.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence and with vendor ranges, labelled as such.
Set a minimum charge for small touch-up and call-out visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A painting rate depends on skill and finish quality, experience, how scarce the work is locally, the range of services a client can book in one visit (interior, exterior, minor plaster repair and decorative finishes), and the cost of running the business. A painter who can take on preparation, small repairs and repainting in one visit may justify a higher rate, because the client saves a second trade visit. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly, rather than cut it to win work. A TradeRefer vendor page gives a national range of $40 to $70 an hour for painting labour (undated page). Treat that as a sense-check only, because it is a lead-referral listing and not an independent benchmark. The owner's own costs and billable hours come first.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel, quoting, colour consultations, admin, marketing, training, cleaning equipment, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, which is a general range and not an Australian painting figure (Jobber, What are billable hours, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026). If only 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, the costs of all 100 hours must come out of the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. Check your own log against the range.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, vehicle, equipment and its upkeep, phone, software, marketing, accounting and any registration fees, to the income you need. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for (Choose a pricing strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026). A registered tax agent should confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. An Australian personal-training guide works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then weekly hours, with tax and costs added on top (AIPT, 16 May 2025). Its example figures are not used here. Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for small jobs
instruction.body: Small painting jobs, such as a single wall touch-up or one door, can cost more in time than they earn, because travel, setup, colour matching and cleanup do not shrink with the size of the job. A minimum charge or call-out fee covers the visit. One contractor guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, setup and cleanup. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). State the minimum before the visit, and explain it to the client in plain terms.

instruction.heading: Reviewing and raising rates
instruction.body: Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months, to check that they still suit the business and its customers (Develop a pricing strategy, no date shown on the page). Raise rates at least once a year to allow for cost and market change. Give repeat clients notice of a new rate, and honour quotes already approved at the old rate. Competitor rates are a guide, not a target. Compare only with insured, licensed, professional painters, because licences, insurance and costs differ.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, setup and admin for a small job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A painter plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed. The painter's log for one month (hypothetical, for this lesson) shows that about 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: If costs and income are divided by all paid hours, the rate looks lower than it should, because the costs still have to come out of the 60 billable hours. The painter builds the rate from billable hours, compares it with the vendor range and the local evidence, checks the minimum charge, and then publishes it with a review date. The factor of about 1.67 is arithmetic from the hypothetical log (100 divided by 60). It is not a sourced figure.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month, with the job type
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a vendor listing or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking small touch-up jobs at the hourly rate, without covering travel and setup.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, setup and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026). That page does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation with a registered tax agent before the rate is published. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Painting licence and registration rules differ by state, and the job value can decide them. In NSW the licence threshold is more than $5,000 in labour and materials including GST. Check the rule for each state where you work before you publish a price sheet.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for small jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: A painter can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average on a website and the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a small painting job?
options: Because a touch-up needs travel but no setup or colour matching at all
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single national average from a vendor listing
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week
